title: Capecitabine + temozolomide (CAPTEM)
context_label: Locally advanced or metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour under NCCP 00505a.
purpose: CAPTEM combines two oral chemotherapy medicines to help control an advanced pancreatic NET. The team discusses the intended benefit, side effects and alternatives. NCCP identifies this pancreatic NET use as outside the medicines’ licences, requiring the local consent process.
schedule_summary: Each cycle lasts 28 days: capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14; add temozolomide once daily on Days 10–14; take neither anticancer medicine on Days 15–28. NCCP plans six cycles unless progression or unacceptable toxicity changes the plan.
scope_note: This guide is for the NCCP pancreatic NET CAPTEM schedule, not a temozolomide brain-tumour or radiotherapy schedule.
schedule_label: 28 days: capecitabine D1–14, temozolomide D10–14, then rest D15–28
indication_text: NCCP 00505a: locally advanced or metastatic pancreatic NET; source eligibility ECOG 0–1. Off-label consent under local policy.
phases_note: The two medicines overlap only on Days 10–14. Six cycles are planned; dose changes, holds or stopping depend on your team’s assessment.
timeline_note: Treatment timing is shown for orientation. Symptoms can develop on any day; no symptom band predicts an individual toxicity peak.
safety_note: Follow your oncology unit’s emergency instructions. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice; do not wait for the next appointment. Call emergency services for collapse, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain or uncontrolled bleeding.
teachback: Can you point out the capecitabine days, the five temozolomide days, the different food instructions and your anti-sickness plan? What symptoms mean stop tablets and call?
consent_support: Discuss the off-label pancreatic NET use, evidence and alternatives, DPD testing, two different oral schedules, nausea prevention on temozolomide days, blood and liver monitoring including after cycles, infection/PJP, fertility and pregnancy precautions.
urgent_extra: Stop capecitabine and contact oncology for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth or hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, vomiting that prevents drinking, fever or sudden illness. Call urgently for new cough/breathlessness, bleeding or yellow skin/eyes. Chest pain or severe breathlessness needs emergency help. Do not restart held treatment without instructions.

agents.name: Capecitabine
agents.mechanism: Converted to fluorouracil inside the body
agents.explanation: Capecitabine is changed into fluorouracil, which interferes with the processes cells use to make and use their genetic instructions. This can damage cancer cells, but healthy bowel, mouth, skin and blood-forming cells can also be affected.
agents.watch: Stop and call for significant diarrhoea, mouth or hand-foot symptoms; chest pain needs emergency assessment.
risks: Severe early toxicity with DPD deficiency

agents.name: Temozolomide
agents.explanation: Temozolomide produces DNA damage that can prevent cancer cells from continuing to grow. Blood-forming cells and other healthy tissues can also be affected, so nausea prevention, blood counts, infection awareness and liver tests are important.
agents.watch: Take the prescribed anti-sickness plan on temozolomide days; report fever, bleeding, new breathing symptoms or liver symptoms.
risks: Low blood counts and delayed marrow suppression
Liver injury, which may be delayed

passport_visit_note: Record both medicines separately, including days and doses held, anti-sickness medicines, blood/liver tests and the next authorised cycle. A stamp records treatment; it does not authorise another cycle.
anatomy: Fatigue or headache can affect daily tasks. Report marked new symptoms; sudden confusion, collapse or a seizure needs emergency help.
Mouth pain or ulcers can prevent eating and drinking. Stop capecitabine and contact the team if symptoms are significant.
Chest pain, pressure or severe breathlessness needs emergency assessment. Tell staff you are taking capecitabine.
Counts can fall, including after capsule days finish. Fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bruising or bleeding needs urgent advice.
New cough, breathlessness or fever needs prompt review. The team considers infection, including PJP, and any prevention plan.
Liver injury can develop during or after treatment. Attend tests after each cycle and report yellow skin/eyes or dark urine.
Diarrhoea or vomiting can cause dehydration. Take prescribed anti-sickness medicine and call for persistent symptoms or reduced urine.
Painful redness, swelling or blisters can limit walking or hand use. Stop capecitabine and call when symptoms are significant.
anatomy_note: Selected regimen-specific effects anchored to the full-body illustration. Blood, hormone and skin effects can involve more than one area. This is not a prediction or a complete side-effect list.
administration_text: The source starting schedule is capecitabine 750 mg/m² twice daily on Days 1–14 and temozolomide 200 mg/m² once daily on Days 10–14 of a 28-day cycle. Your own label gives the actual tablet/capsule numbers. Take capecitabine with food or within 30 minutes afterwards; take temozolomide fasting according to the pharmacy instructions. Swallow both whole; do not crush, cut or open them.

phases.label: CAPTEM · six planned 28-day cycles
phases.detail: Each cycle lasts 28 days: capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14; add temozolomide once daily on Days 10–14; take neither anticancer medicine on Days 15–28. NCCP plans six cycles unless progression or unacceptable toxicity changes the plan.

timeline.label: Capecitabine twice daily
timeline.text: With food or within 30 minutes after food.

timeline.label: Temozolomide once daily
timeline.text: Fasting; follow the separate anti-sickness plan.

timeline.label: No CAPTEM tablets / capsules
timeline.text: Recovery, liver tests and next-cycle assessment.

timeline.label: Symptoms and safety
timeline.text: Serious symptoms can occur during rest days too.

day_groups.title: Capecitabine only
day_groups.body: Take the prescribed morning and evening doses with food or within 30 minutes afterwards.
day_groups.action: Check your calendar and report bowel, mouth or hand-foot symptoms early.

day_groups.title: Both medicines; different food instructions
day_groups.body: Continue capecitabine twice daily. Add the once-daily temozolomide dose fasting, with the prescribed anti-sickness plan.
day_groups.action: Ask the pharmacist to write practical dose and meal times; do not assume both medicines are taken together.

day_groups.title: Planned rest from both anticancer medicines
day_groups.body: Take neither CAPTEM medicine unless the team has changed your written plan. Symptoms and low blood counts may continue.
day_groups.action: Complete liver tests after the cycle and blood tests before the next. Restart only when authorised.

support.title: Separate nausea-prevention plan
support.text: Capecitabine is minimal-to-low emetogenic, while temozolomide is moderate-to-high emetogenic in this oral schedule. The team must prescribe an oral anti-sickness plan for Days 10–14 and any rescue treatment; this is not a single low-risk infusion plan.

support.title: Mouth, hands and feet
support.text: Use the unit’s mouth and skin care. Significant pain, ulcers or hand-foot symptoms may require capecitabine interruption; do not keep taking tablets just to finish the fortnight.

support.title: Diarrhoea and fluids
support.text: Ask for written diarrhoea instructions and the point at which to stop capecitabine and call. Persistent vomiting, severe diarrhoea, dizziness or inability to drink needs urgent advice.

support.title: Infection and PJP prevention
support.text: The team assesses whether PJP prevention is needed under local policy, especially with steroid exposure or other risk factors. CAPTEM is not the 42-day temozolomide-plus-radiotherapy schedule; do not borrow that schedule’s automatic prevention plan.

monitoring_schedule.title: Safety tests before, between and after CAPTEM cycles

rows.label: Blood count / kidneys / liver
cells: FBC, renal and liver profile
Before each cycle; liver tests also after each cycle
Earlier assessment for infection, bleeding, dehydration or symptoms
Review recovery before another cycle
Liver effects may arise weeks after the final dose

rows.label: DPD / hepatitis B / INR
cells: DPD before capecitabine unless already tested; hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody
INR if indicated, especially with warfarin
Watch for unusually severe early toxicity
Specialist review of any DPD-related risk or interacting medicine
Follow specialist and anticoagulation plans

rows.label: Symptoms / oral medicines
cells: Record usual bowel pattern, intake, mouth, skin and activity
Review adherence, worst symptoms and any doses held
Nausea plan on D10–14; symptom calls on all days
Confirm both prescriptions and the next start date
Follow persistent symptoms and return unused medicine

rows.label: NET response / duration
cells: Confirm pancreatic NET, goal and six-cycle plan
Scans / hormone markers according to the consultant plan
Track symptoms; report change without waiting for imaging
Balance response, toxicity and patient goals
Discuss follow-up or next treatment after the intended course

monitoring_schedule.note: Six cycles are planned in NCCP; the team may change or stop treatment for progression or toxicity. Do not substitute a fixed scan/marker timetable from another NET treatment.

monitoring_summary: Before starting: blood count, kidney/liver tests, hepatitis B screening and DPD testing unless already tested. Blood count, kidney and liver tests before every cycle; liver tests also after each cycle. INR if indicated with warfarin. Liver injury can appear weeks after the last dose. Scans and hormone markers follow the consultant plan.

chronology_notes.title: Two calendars in one cycle
chronology_notes.text: Capecitabine starts on Day 1; temozolomide starts on Day 10. The overlap lasts five days, then both stop for Days 15–28.

chronology_notes.title: Rest days still need symptom awareness
chronology_notes.text: Blood counts and other effects may worsen after the tablets finish. Continue the emergency plan throughout the cycle.

chronology_notes.title: Delayed liver effects
chronology_notes.text: Keep the arranged liver tests after each cycle and any follow-up after the last dose; do not assume all risks end on Day 14.

sections.title: Dose and meal timing
sections.text: The source starting schedule is capecitabine 750 mg/m² twice daily on Days 1–14 and temozolomide 200 mg/m² once daily on Days 10–14 of a 28-day cycle. Your own label gives the actual tablet/capsule numbers. Take capecitabine with food or within 30 minutes afterwards; take temozolomide fasting according to the pharmacy instructions. Swallow both whole; do not crush, cut or open them.

sections.title: Missed or vomited doses
sections.text: Do not double capecitabine or take a replacement dose after vomiting. If you miss temozolomide, follow the pharmacy’s written instructions or call before taking it late. If you vomit after temozolomide, do not take a second dose that day. Never replace doses omitted because of toxicity.

sections.title: Support medicines
sections.text: Have the Days 10–14 anti-sickness prescription ready before Day 10. Ask how it fits around fasting temozolomide and meals for capecitabine. Follow the local rescue and constipation/diarrhoea plan.

sections.title: Medicine interactions
sections.text: Bring a complete medicine list. Warfarin may need extra INR checks. Tell the team about seizure medicines and recent brivudine or related antiviral treatment; dangerous interactions require specialist review.

sections.title: Storage and handling
sections.text: Keep each medicine in its own labelled original packaging and away from children. Do not cut or crush capecitabine or open temozolomide capsules. If swallowing is difficult, contact pharmacy before treatment. Return unused medicine as advised.

sections.title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility
sections.text: These medicines can harm a pregnancy and may affect fertility. Discuss contraception for patients and partners, the required duration after the last dose, fertility preservation and breastfeeding before starting; follow the medicine-specific written plan.

sections.title: Review appointments
sections.text: Before starting: blood count, kidney/liver tests, hepatitis B screening and DPD testing unless already tested. Blood count, kidney and liver tests before every cycle; liver tests also after each cycle. INR if indicated with warfarin. Liver injury can appear weeks after the last dose. Scans and hormone markers follow the consultant plan.

evidence.title: Evidence for the pancreatic NET combination
evidence.intro: ECOG-ACRIN E2211 compared CAPTEM with temozolomide alone.
evidence.population: A randomised phase II study in advanced low- or intermediate-grade pancreatic NET with recent progression.
evidence.interpretation: Adding capecitabine improved the time before disease progression in the trial.
limitations: The final overall-survival comparison was not statistically significant. Progression-free survival is not a personal survival forecast.
The study population and trial treatment duration do not replace the Irish six-cycle regimen, consent process or individual decision. Routine MGMT testing is not mandated by this source.

chapters.title: Your CAPTEM treatment
chapters.intro: Two chemotherapy medicines with carefully separated instructions.

items.title: Why CAPTEM?
items.text: CAPTEM combines two oral chemotherapy medicines to help control an advanced pancreatic NET. The team discusses the intended benefit, side effects and alternatives. NCCP identifies this pancreatic NET use as outside the medicines’ licences, requiring the local consent process.

items.title: What the medicines do
items.text: Capecitabine is changed into fluorouracil, which interferes with the processes cells use to make and use their genetic instructions. This can damage cancer cells, but healthy bowel, mouth, skin and blood-forming cells can also be affected. Temozolomide produces DNA damage that can prevent cancer cells from continuing to grow. Blood-forming cells and other healthy tissues can also be affected, so nausea prevention, blood counts, infection awareness and liver tests are important.

items.title: Schedule and planned duration
items.text: Each cycle lasts 28 days: capecitabine twice daily on Days 1–14; add temozolomide once daily on Days 10–14; take neither anticancer medicine on Days 15–28. NCCP plans six cycles unless progression or unacceptable toxicity changes the plan.

items.title: Evidence and uncertainty
items.text: Adding capecitabine improved the time before disease progression in the trial. The final overall-survival comparison was not statistically significant. Progression-free survival is not a personal survival forecast. The study population and trial treatment duration do not replace the Irish six-cycle regimen, consent process or individual decision. Routine MGMT testing is not mandated by this source.

chapters.title: Tests, urgent symptoms and follow-up
chapters.intro: Some effects appear after treatment days have ended.

items.title: Before, during and after cycles
items.text: Before starting: blood count, kidney/liver tests, hepatitis B screening and DPD testing unless already tested. Blood count, kidney and liver tests before every cycle; liver tests also after each cycle. INR if indicated with warfarin. Liver injury can appear weeks after the last dose. Scans and hormone markers follow the consultant plan.

items.title: When to stop and call
items.text: Stop capecitabine and contact oncology for significant diarrhoea, painful mouth or hand-foot symptoms affecting activity, vomiting that prevents drinking, fever or sudden illness. Call urgently for new cough/breathlessness, bleeding or yellow skin/eyes. Chest pain or severe breathlessness needs emergency help. Do not restart held treatment without instructions.

items.title: Unusually severe early effects
items.text: DPD helps break down capecitabine’s active drug. DPD testing reduces risk but does not remove it. Severe early diarrhoea, mouth soreness, infection or neurological symptoms needs immediate team assessment; do not continue waiting for the next cycle.

items.title: Storage and handling
items.text: Keep each medicine in its own labelled original packaging and away from children. Do not cut or crush capecitabine or open temozolomide capsules. If swallowing is difficult, contact pharmacy before treatment. Return unused medicine as advised.

items.text: These medicines can harm a pregnancy and may affect fertility. Discuss contraception for patients and partners, the required duration after the last dose, fertility preservation and breastfeeding before starting; follow the medicine-specific written plan.

chapters.title: Understanding your particular NET
chapters.intro: Several different features help the team choose treatment.

items.title: Where it started and where it is now
items.text: A neuroendocrine tumour begins in cells with hormone-making features. Its starting organ and the places it has spread are separate parts of the diagnosis. A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour differs from pancreatic adenocarcinoma; a deposit in the liver may have come from another organ.

items.title: Differentiation, grade and Ki-67
items.text: The pathology report describes how organised the cells look (differentiation) and their growth activity (grade). Ki-67 measures cells showing a growth-related protein in the sample. Its percentage describes that sample, not the amount of your body affected or your chance of survival.

items.title: Grade is different from stage
items.text: Stage describes extent; grade describes tumour biology. Either can vary independently. A well-differentiated grade 3 neuroendocrine tumour and a poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma are distinct diagnoses and may need different treatments.

items.title: Functioning and nonfunctioning
items.text: A functioning tumour produces a hormone syndrome. A nonfunctioning tumour can still cause problems through growth or pressure. Somatostatin receptor uptake on a scan shows a treatment target; it does not, on its own, identify a hormone syndrome.

items.title: Your diagnosis record
items.text: Ask for one diagnosis summary: starting organ, grade, differentiation, Ki-67 result if reported, sites involved, hormone syndrome and receptor-imaging result. Keep pending results clearly marked.

chapters.title: Making sense of tests and results
chapters.intro: Safety tests, tumour tests and hormone tests answer different questions.

items.title: Blood tests for treatment safety
items.text: Blood counts assess oxygen-carrying cells, infection-fighting cells and platelets. Kidney and liver results help assess treatment safety. These checks are needed even when you feel well; a reassuring scan answers a different question.

items.title: CT, MRI and receptor imaging
items.text: CT and MRI show anatomy and tumour size. Somatostatin receptor imaging tests whether a particular receptor target is present. An FDG-PET scan measures uptake of a glucose-like tracer and is used selectively. Your team chooses the scans that can guide your care.

items.title: Hormones and tumour markers are individual
items.text: Selected markers may help answer a hormone or tumour question. Examples include 5-HIAA for serotonin-related symptoms, chromogranin A, or a specific pancreatic hormone. They are not a routine panel for every neuroendocrine tumour. Interpret changes with symptoms and imaging.

items.title: Preparing for a test
items.text: Use the laboratory instructions for fasting, food restrictions and any timed urine collection. Some medicines affect marker results, including acid-suppressing medicines and chromogranin A. Ask the team what to do; do not stop a prescribed medicine yourself.

items.title: Heart and inherited-risk checks
items.text: Some hormone syndromes can affect heart valves, so an ultrasound of the heart may be requested. Inherited-risk assessment depends on the tumour and family history; multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is one example. An inherited-risk test and a test of tumour tissue answer different questions.

items.title: Who does what, and when?
items.text: For each test, write its name, purpose, booking date and result-review contact. Ask the team to set your next scan or marker date. A schedule for someone after surgery may not apply during your treatment.

chapters.title: Hormone symptoms and day-to-day changes
chapters.intro: A new symptom may come from the NET, treatment or another illness.

items.title: Build a picture of what is normal for you
items.text: Keep a brief record of your usual bowel pattern, flushing, appetite, weight, pain and energy. Note new changes and when they started. This helps the team assess whether treatment, hormones or another problem needs attention.

items.title: Hormone-related symptoms
items.text: Hormone symptoms depend on the tumour: examples include flushing and watery diarrhoea, acid-related symptoms, or changes in blood sugar. An insulin-producing tumour can lower blood sugar. Ask which symptoms apply to you and whether you need a written rescue plan.

items.title: Hormone treatment is a separate part of the plan
items.text: Hormone-control medicines have their own schedule. A pause in anticancer tablets does not automatically mean pausing those medicines. Before peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, the specialist team coordinates any interruption and restart of somatostatin analogue injections.

items.title: When a change is urgent
items.text: Follow your oncology emergency plan for sudden or severe symptoms. Collapse, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, confusion or uncontrolled bleeding needs emergency assessment. Severe diarrhoea, persistent vomiting, dehydration, fever or sudden illness needs urgent oncology advice. Do not wait for a scan, an online answer or the next clinic visit.

items.title: Procedures and hormone syndromes
items.text: Tell teams arranging an operation, anaesthetic or other procedure about a hormone-producing tumour or previous hormone crisis. Your specialist decides whether extra preparation is needed. Carry the agreed emergency instructions and current medicine list.

chapters.title: Your overall plan and choices
chapters.intro: Your priorities belong in the treatment plan.

items.title: What are we trying to achieve?
items.text: Agree your treatment aim: slowing growth, reducing tumour size, controlling hormone symptoms or preserving daily function. A scan showing no growth may be a useful result even when the tumour has not shrunk.

items.title: How treatments fit together
items.text: Your plan may use different treatments at different times, including surgery, medicines, receptor-targeted radiation or treatment directed at the liver. Ask the team to mark your own sequence and who coordinates it.

items.title: Choosing between options
items.text: Ask why the proposed option fits the tumour site, grade, receptor findings, symptoms and your health. Discuss reasonable alternatives, observation when appropriate and suitable trials. Your team explains which options are available to you.

items.title: Evidence is about groups
items.text: Studies measure different outcomes, such as shrinkage, time before worsening and survival. Ask which outcome matters for your plan and how closely the study group matches your diagnosis. No study average can predict one person’s course.

items.title: Review points and shared decisions
items.text: Agree when to review the plan and what could lead to continuing, pausing or changing treatment. Include the effects on work, caring duties, travel and the activities that matter to you.

chapters.title: Eating, energy, practical help and support
chapters.intro: Supportive care can be used alongside treatment from the start.

items.title: Food, weight and digestion
items.text: Report weight loss, persistent diarrhoea, greasy stools or difficulty eating. Different causes need different treatment. Ask for a dietitian and whether reduced digestive-enzyme function needs assessment.

items.title: Fluids and safe activity
items.text: Use your personal fluid advice, especially with diarrhoea or heart or kidney disease. Adjust activity and rest to your energy. Report dizziness, breathlessness or fatigue that limits daily tasks so treatable causes can be checked.

items.title: Emotions, relationships and quality of life
items.text: Ask for help with mood, sleep, relationships, intimacy or caring responsibilities when you need it. Symptom and palliative-care teams can support comfort and quality of life while anticancer treatment continues.

items.title: Practical help
items.text: Ask your specialist nurse or social worker about transport, employment, finances and help at home. Tell them about caring responsibilities and ask which support organisations fit your needs.

items.title: A record that works without a phone
items.text: Keep a paper schedule, current medicine list and real contact numbers together. The handbook can be read without internet access. Use the written emergency plan whenever you need urgent help.

items.title: Questions to take to the next visit
items.text: For the next visit, choose the questions that matter most: my exact diagnosis; the aim of treatment; which tests I need and why; who explains results; when to call; and what help is available.

questions.q: What is the aim of CAPTEM, and how was its off-label use explained?
questions.a: Ask the team to explain the expected benefit, alternatives and burdens for your pancreatic NET. NCCP identifies this use as off-label and requires the local consent process.

questions.q: Has my DPD result been reviewed?
questions.a: DPD testing is required before first capecitabine unless already completed. Ask the team to confirm the result and any special plan; testing does not remove every risk of severe toxicity.

questions.q: Can you write exact dose and meal times for Days 10–14?
questions.a: Ask the pharmacist to write a practical calendar. Capecitabine is taken with food or within 30 minutes afterwards; temozolomide is taken fasting. Do not assume the two medicines should be swallowed together.

questions.q: What anti-sickness medicines should I take on temozolomide days?
questions.a: Temozolomide Days 10–14 has moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Your team must prescribe the local preventive and rescue plan and explain its timing; this guide does not select a universal drug or dose.

questions.q: When are liver tests after each cycle and after the last dose?
questions.a: Liver tests are needed before and after each cycle. Injury may occur weeks after the final dose, so ask for the follow-up dates and whom to call for yellow skin/eyes or dark urine.

questions.q: Which symptoms mean stop capecitabine and call?
questions.a: Significant diarrhoea, mouth pain or hand-foot symptoms, vomiting that prevents drinking, fever or sudden illness needs prompt advice and capecitabine interruption as instructed. Chest pain or severe breathlessness needs emergency assessment.

questions.q: When will we review the six-cycle plan and response?
questions.a: The NCCP plan is six 28-day cycles unless progression or unacceptable toxicity changes it. Your consultant decides response-scan timing and whether the course should continue or change.

monitoring_test_details.timing: Only if requested for your hormone syndrome; the team sets the dates.

monitoring_test_details.detail: Often a timed urine collection. Follow the laboratory’s food and medicine instructions.

monitoring_test_details.label: Chromogranin A
monitoring_test_details.timing: Only when the team considers it informative for your tumour.
monitoring_test_details.purpose: A selected tumour-marker result, interpreted with symptoms and scans.
monitoring_test_details.detail: Acid-suppressing medicines and other conditions can alter the result. It is not a routine test before every treatment; do not stop medicines yourself.
